newsitem.title: USA: Auditors say Miami port's problems go back many years.
newsitem.headline: Auditors say Miami port's problems go back many years.

text.p: Auditors looking into the scandal-hit Port of Miami said on Wednesday they rang alarm bells years ago that it was awash in financial problems but authorities ignored the warnings.

Responding to questions on the latest scandal to plague the self-styled "Magic City," the auditors told county commissioners they had repeatedly warned in annual reports and letters to management that the seaport had operating losses and many uncollected debts.

"The applicable numbers were disclosed year in and year out. It certainly hasn't shown any optimistic portrayal of anything," Ron Jones of Deloitte & Touche, told the Dade County Commission's maritime trade committee.

The problems at the port -- the world's busiest cruise ship harbor and a major cargo hub -- emerged with revelations that seaport revenues had been spent on Super Bowl tickets, luxury car rentals, charity golf tournaments, and political campaign contributions.
Port director Carmen Lunetta, 67, tendered his resignation on Friday, hours after embarrassing documents were made public.

The scandal is the latest in a wave that has broken over Miami in the past year, including a City Hall corruption and bribery affair and the discovery that the city had a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for fiscal 1997.

Commissioners for Dade County, which runs the port, called the auditors in on Wednesday to question why they only learned last week that the seaport had a $22 million cash flow deficit and that it had borrowed $37 million from the county general fund over several years to keep operating.
"The auditors have to sound a loud bell at the smell of a rat," Commissioner Miriam Alonso said. "In this case the rat has been dead a long time."

But the auditors pointed to the annual reports they submitted to the county. The reports showed the seaport had operating losses in seven of the last 10 years, with the annual losses ranging from $840,000 to $7.8 million.
The management letters said many seaport customers routinely failed to pay their bills within 90 days, and urged the port to adopt tougher collections procedures.

Every year the seaport replied that it agreed with the recommendation but that it had trouble collecting debts during times of economic hardship, another Deloitte auditor, Susan Tripp, told the commmission.

Alonso also confirmed on Wednesday that the Miami U.S. Attorney's Office is investigating the relationship between Fiscal Operations, the company that operates the cargo cranes, and Lunetta and the port.

Tripp said auditors thought it odd that cargo revenues had dropped when more cranes had been added. Fiscal Operations also owes Dade County $24 million but it was unlikely the county could collect, she said.
Asked whether he and other officials should have realized earlier that the port was in the red, county manager Armando Vidal said: "I don't think finger-pointing is the issue."
In an editorial headlined "The Party's Over", Wednesday's Miami Herald said: "Lunetta spread the wealth to keep officials content to ignore his lack of accountability."
But his fall from grace had a soft landing. The Herald reported that he will receive a package totalling more than $328,500 in benefits and a pension of $113,000 per year.
The port's woes came to light as Miami voters prepared for a Sept. 4 referendum on a proposal to dissolve the city and merge it into the Dade County government.

The city of Miami is only a fragment of the urban sprawl generally known by that name. Most of the greater Miami area is actually run by Dade County authorities or is part of separate cities such as Coral Gables and Miami Beach.
